In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the number of queries needed by the search engine to find a collection of documents represented as a conjunction of relevant attributes is at most 2n+1, and the number of queries to find a collection represented as a disjunction of relevant attributes is O(n).
for a given concept class, the number of queries needed for learning with equivalence queries is at most twice the number of queries required for learning with membership queries.

, in the worst case, the number of queries needed by a search engine to search for a disjunction of relevant attributes is exponential in the number of relevant attributes, and the number of queries is linear in the number of attributes when the relevant attributes are a conjunction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to search the Web with a small number of queries, even in the case of large n. Our algorithms are efficient, and can be implemented in practice.

, if the collection of documents can be represented as a disjunction (conjunction) of a small number of attributes, then the search engine can search for the collection by making a small (polynomial) number of queries from the user.

, for any collection of Web documents, the number of queries that a search engine needs to learn the collection is at most O(n), which is optimal for the class of disjunctions (or conjunctions) of n boolean attributes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of queries that a search engine needs is independent of the number of Web documents.
, in the worst case, the number of queries needed by our algorithms is optimal, and our algorithms can be implemented in polynomial time.
the number of queries needed by a learner is independent of the size of the Web and is linear in the size of the target concept.
